title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
trick: Have a coding agent write each robot simulation's physics itself, then make same-model auditor agents re-run its measurements and attack it with legal robot actions for three rounds; ship whatever survives as RL environments.
framing_stripped: Called 'a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations' grounded in U.S. GDP data; it is a Claude Opus 5.5 creation-audit loop (one creator, four auditors incl. an adversarial one, three rounds, shared Markdown memory; Appendix B) that produced 25 simulations with agent-written solvers for liquids, cloth, molten metal, soil, paste, tissue and sound, 200 tasks with deterministic state-based verifiers, plus a benchmark result (frontier models score 0% success on the 25 test tasks under a 3-hour wall-clock budget) and four in-context-learning studies that exploit privileged simulator state (sec. 3, 4, 5, 6).
method_equations: Action weighting (Appendix A, eq. 1): $W(a) = \sum_{t} W(t)\, P_{\mathrm{phys}}(t)\, R(a \mid t)$ with $\sum_a R(a \mid t) = 1$, where $W(t)$ is the economic value of task $t$ (wage bill from BLS employment $\times$ mean wage scaled to BEA accounts, or population-hours from the American Time Use Survey), $P_{\mathrm{phys}}(t) \in [0,1]$ is the LLM-estimated fraction of $t$ that is physical, and $R(a \mid t)$ is the LLM-attributed share of $t$'s physical execution carried by atomic action $a$. Coverage of a selected set of action groups $S$ on an activity slice $Q$ (eq. 2): $F_Q(S) = \frac{\sum_a V_{Q,a}\, y_a(S)}{\sum_a V_{Q,a}}$, where $V_{Q,a}$ is the value of action $a$ inside $Q$ and $y_a(S) = 1$ if every capability $a$ requires is supplied by some group in $S$, else $0$; each of six tiers is solved as an exact batch optimisation maximising the coverage it adds (120 groups selected, 25 built). A task (sec. 2.1) is $T = (E_{s_0}, p, V)$: simulation $E$ at initial state $s_0$, instruction $p$, verifier $V$ mapping the episode's physical states to a success bit and a reward $r \in [0,1]$ with $r = 1$ on every valid completion. Interaction: at step $t$ the agent sees $o_t$ (camera images, robot feedback) and issues command $a_t$; physics advances only while $a_t$ executes (command-driven clock). Reported metrics (sec. 6.1): success rate $= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}[V_i = \text{success}]$ and average reward $= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} r_i$ over $N$ attempts. The 'physics checks' column (Table 1, Table 6) is a count $n_{\mathrm{pc}}(E)$ of named experiments in $E$'s own report 'that test its physics against theory, measurement, or expected behavior'; no tolerance, pass criterion or error statistic is defined for a check. The speed criterion (Appendix B) is $\tau_{\mathrm{sim}} / \tau_{\mathrm{real}} \le 200$, the simulation at most 200 times slower than real time.
load_bearing_assumption: That a physics model written by a coding agent is realistic once auditor agents of the same model have (a) re-run the creator's own named checks against formulas, datasheets and 'expected behavior', (b) watched its videos with a video model, and (c) failed to break it with legal robot actions in three rounds. If a simulation can pass all ten criteria while its contact or material dynamics are wrong in ways only a higher-fidelity reference solve or real measurements would reveal, then 'realistic' means 'self-consistent and audit-passing', the 76% physics win rate (Figure 9) is one model's preference for its own kind of report, and the GDP-coverage claim $F_Q(S)$ counts coverage of physics nobody has validated. The paper offers no real-robot or real-measurement comparison for any of the 25 simulations: 'Physics checks count the named experiments in each simulation's report that test its physics against theory, measurement, or expected behavior' (Appendix E), and the VLA result ends with a policy 'that can in principle be deployed on a real robot' (sec. 6.3).
weakest_component: A closed evidence chain in which one model plays every role: Claude Opus 5.5 is the creator, all four auditors, the difficulty calibrator (with Haiku 5.5), the blind judge of the 25 prior-simulator comparisons ('Claude Opus 5.5 then compared each pair blind', sec. 6.4), and one of the three benchmarked agents. A critic attacks it first because (1) the headline quality numbers (76% physics win, 80% visuals win) are a same-model preference judgment over reports and videos, not a measurement; (2) the adversarial auditor 'found a real defect in about three quarters of our simulations' (sec. 6.4) and the shared memory records 'colliders that passed audits and appeared in renders while having no physical effect' (Appendix B), so the residual defect rate after three rounds is bounded only by that auditor's recall, which is never estimated; (3) the 0% / 0.06-reward headline is produced under a 3-hour wall-clock budget with a step-by-step LLM controller and a harness-specific tool set, so it measures harness, budget and degrees of freedom (Table 3: humanoids 0% for two of three models) as much as physical competence; (4) solver settings are chosen by the agent per simulation (0.5 ms ticks on Newton 1.5 / MuJoCo Warp; 1,920 Hz with 64 solver iterations for the padlock; 1e-5 s substeps for FEM filleting; Table 6) with one named convergence check in 25 ('ink timestep and resolution convergence', whiteboard) and a 'heuristic' temperature model in ingredient mixing; no simulation reports a step-size or iteration-count convergence study on the states a policy visits.
regime: 25 agent-built simulations, 200 RL environments (25 test, 175 train, plus an 'easier' 25 from train), each with swappable robots (FR3, Panda, UR10e, Mobile FR3 Duo, Unitree G1 and H1-2; 8 to 43 DoF) and variations of pose, appearance and physics. Engines mixed per simulation behind one HTTP interface: Newton 1.5 with the MuJoCo Warp solver, Warp custom solvers (DFSPH liquids with 93,750-348,160 particles, MPM soil, backward-Euler cloth, explicit FEM tissue with 73,273 tets), a 7.18 M-cell GPU enthalpy solver for welding, PhysX in some prior-comparison rows. Speed bound: at most 200x slower than real time. Benchmarked agents: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Terra, Claude Opus 5.5 at extra-high reasoning effort, each in its own harness (Codex, Claude Code), restricted access, one 3-hour attempt per task; results: 0% success on all 25 test tasks, average reward 0.002-0.06; easier subset 12-32% success, reward 0.17-0.48 (Figure 6, Table 3). Learning study: Opus 5.5 on 11 simulations, three 3-hour attempts; solo 0.14 to 0.22, privileged 0.34 to 0.41, coached student 0.29 first attempt, self-transfer 0.17 to 0.29 (Figure 7). VLA: code policies succeed on 96.7% of 2,048 varied gift-box states; 1,000 demos train $\pi_{0.5}$ from 0% to 53% (55% on unseen variations), 2 min per task vs 29 min for Opus step-by-step. Creation cost: all agents Claude Opus 5.5, three audit rounds per simulation, difficulty calibration with four Haiku seeds and two Opus seeds at six hours each; dollar and GPU cost of building a simulation not reported. No RL training run in the paper; no real-robot result.
information_asymmetry: (1) Creation vs reference: at creation and audit time the only physics evidence is what the creator chose to measure and the auditor chose to re-run, both from the same model, against references the creator picked (a formula, a datasheet, 'expected behavior'); what is missing is an independent reference for the dynamic contact regime the tasks live in. That reference exists in two places the paper never touches: a higher-fidelity re-solve of the same scene (halved time step, more solver iterations, a second contact model) on the states actually visited, which the released code and the documented solver settings make possible, and real material and impact data the field already holds (RGBench's measured garment dynamics, Acosta et al.'s elastic-impact data, the GAUGE material tables) which the creator cites for static parameters but never uses to check a trajectory. The L5 audit $d_t = \lVert F_{\mathrm{ref}}(x_t, u_t) - x_{t+1} \rVert$ on recorded rollouts has not been run on any agent-written simulator; this paper is the first corpus of 25 such simulators with every attempt recorded ('Every attempt records each command request and response, the camera images at command boundaries, the launch configuration and source version, and the final evaluation', Appendix D), so the rollouts to audit exist and the audit does not. (2) Pre-training exploit search vs under-optimisation exploit: the adversarial auditor searches for exploits before any policy is optimised against the simulation, with a model's imagination of legal actions and a three-round budget; the paper's own warning is that 'Since reinforcement learning optimizes against the simulation, any such exploit could otherwise become learned behavior' (sec. 3), yet no RL is run on the 175 training environments, so the exploit share of return under optimisation pressure, the quantity L5 calls $\rho$, is unmeasured. The one optimised policy family (code policies, 2,048 rollouts, 96.7% success) is the cheapest place to measure it. (3) Count vs content: Tables 1 and 6 report $n_{\mathrm{pc}}$, the number of named checks per simulation (6 to 18), while the checks' pass criteria, tolerances and errors live only in the agent-written reports; a reader cannot tell a 2% from a 40% miss. (4) Per-simulation vs per-engine: each simulation picks its own engine and solver settings, documented in Table 6, but nothing aggregates across the 25 to say which engine or which setting family the audits flagged; the agent-chosen iteration caps and time steps are exactly the knobs L5 says trade physics for speed, and the 200x-slower-than-real-time bound is the only speed constraint, so there is no speed-fidelity frontier for any of them. (5) Judge vs instrument: the blind comparison that yields 76% is a model reading two simulators' artifacts; the instrument that would replace it, matched physical quantities under matched inputs across the two simulators of the same interaction, is what J06's ported-incumbent half would supply.
occupies: Published and released, so no longer claimable: a GDP-weighted selection of 120 physical action groups with a coverage objective; a creation-audit loop in which a frontier coding agent writes task-specific physics solvers (not just scenes on a fixed engine) and auditor agents check them with self-run measurements, assisted demonstrations and adversarial legal actions; 25 non-rigid-heavy simulations with 200 verifier-scored RL environments, swappable robots and physics variations; the result that three frontier models score 0% on the test split; and the privileged-state learning recipes (in-context, coach hints, self-transfer, code-policy demonstrations training $\pi_{0.5}$ from 0% to 53%). From CL-W43-J06 it takes the 'frontier-model-synthesised scenes' half outright: a released, agent-built, non-rigid test suite with a side-by-side table against the incumbents (SoftGym, ManiSkill2, GarmentLab, Chemistry3D, LabUtopia, FluidLab, DaXBench, RGBench, BEHAVIOR-1K; Tables 1, 2, 6) now exists, and 'nobody has such a suite' is no longer a reason to build one. It does not take J06's ported-incumbent half (no incumbent task is ported; incumbents appear only as table rows and as same-model blind-comparison opponents), it does not take the instrument (no physics audit under a reference on visited states), and it does not take CL-W43-J05 (agents here write new solvers to their own speed bound; they do not accelerate a shipped engine at fixed accuracy).

neighbors.title: Gym-Anything: Turn any Software into an Agent Environment
neighbors.trick: Have a coding agent set up real software with real data while an audit agent checks its evidence against a checklist, over 200 GDP-ranked applications, to get 10K computer-use tasks; this card's paper is the same loop with the agent writing the physics instead of configuring an existing program.

neighbors.title: GenSim: Generating Robotic Simulation Tasks via Large Language Models
neighbors.trick: Ask GPT-4 to write new task code and demonstrations on top of a fixed rigid-body simulator, growing a benchmark tenfold to over 100 tasks; the paper positions itself as the step past this, where the agent writes the physics too and checks it with measurements, not policy success.

neighbors.title: RoboGen: Towards Unleashing Infinite Data for Automated Robot Learning via Generative Simulation
neighbors.trick: Let a model propose tasks, populate scenes with assets, decompose into subtasks and pick RL or planning to learn each skill, all on an existing engine's physics; this card's paper says such generators are limited to rigid and articulated objects and verify by inspection, not measurement.

neighbors.title: Real Garment Benchmark (RGBench): A Comprehensive Benchmark for Robotic Garment Manipulation featuring a High-Fidelity Scalable Simulator
neighbors.trick: Build a cloth simulator and score it against carefully measured real garment dynamics (20% lower error, 3x faster than rivals) over 6,000 garment meshes; the only row in the paper's Table 2 with physics checked against real data, and the model for the real-data reference this card's paper lacks.

neighbors.title: BEHAVIOR-1K: A Human-Centered, Embodied AI Benchmark with 1,000 Everyday Activities and Realistic Simulation
neighbors.trick: Choose 1,000 household activities from a survey of what people want robots to do and simulate them with rigid, deformable and liquid physics in OmniGibson, with one sim-to-real transfer study; the paper's 'closest to broad coverage' incumbent, hand-built and survey-grounded rather than agent-built and wage-grounded.

theme_fit.why: scout on 'agent-built simulators': the headline a stranger repeats is that coding agents now write robot physics solvers nobody independently validates, and frontier models score 0.06 on the result; lab-adjacent (CMU, released code), measurement register available, probe-able under one GPU-week

supplies the target corpus and the enabling piece for the lane's audit: 25 simulators with agent-chosen time steps and iteration caps, recorded rollouts, released code and no reference-based verification; it does not itself measure whether those settings trade physics for speed or whether policies exploit them
a benchmark whose headline (0% success) depends on a 3-hour wall-clock budget, harness and robot DoF; validity questions exist but the paper is not an evaluation-infrastructure study

limitations_as_complaints: My adversarial auditor 'found a real defect in about three quarters of our simulations' using only legal robot actions, and my memory file exists because of 'colliders that passed audits and appeared in renders while having no physical effect', so I know my audits miss things and I cannot tell you how many defects remain after round three, or whether an RL policy will find them; I say myself that 'any such exploit could otherwise become learned behavior' but I never train RL on the 175 training environments (sec. 3, sec. 6.4, Appendix B).

My physics quality evidence is a count of experiments my own creation agent named and ran against 'theory, measurement, or expected behavior', plus a win rate from a blind comparison where 'Claude Opus 5.5 then compared each pair blind'; the same model built, audited and judged, no simulation is compared with a real measurement of a trajectory, and my VLA result ends at a policy 'that can in principle be deployed on a real robot' (Table 1, Appendix E, sec. 6.4, sec. 6.3).

My speed auditor 'requires that a simulation run at most 200 times slower than real time', my liquids carry up to 348,160 SPH particles and my welding cell 7.18 M enthalpy cells, and 'a frontier model controls the robot step by step, which is slow and costly' (29 minutes per gift-box task, 3-hour attempts), so I cannot run the thousands of parallel episodes per task that the RL I was built for needs, and I report no GPU cost for building or running a simulation (Appendix B, Table 6, sec. 5, sec. 6.3).
